prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at the magic wavelength made frequency measurement at the 1e-18 level possible

statement.case_for: I keep the same configuration as in round 1: B042 with Katori and Ye, and I have not moved. The exchange has sharpened the reason. The question the chair put to us, which specific new principle separates the lattice clock from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, has a concrete answer. The 2005 prize recognised the frequency comb and precision spectroscopy that make optical frequencies countable. The 2012 prize recognised control of single quantum systems, including the single-ion optical clock. The lattice clock rests on a different idea: choosing a trap wavelength at which the light shift of the clock transition cancels, so that many neutral atoms are held tightly in the Lamb-Dicke regime with neither Doppler nor recoil broadening and the statistical power of a large ensemble is gained without giving up accuracy. That idea is not a refinement of a comb or of an ion trap. It has been realised independently in Sr, Yb and Hg and compared between laboratories at about 1e-18, so the result does not depend on one group. As a microscopist I note how rarely a metrology result survives that kind of cross-laboratory test; here it has, and that is the evidence I trust most. The prize is for a discovery or invention, in the sense used for the physics prize, and this is an invention with a named originator (Katori, the magic-wavelength proposal and early demonstration) and a named person who carried the many-atom architecture to the lowest systematic uncertainty (Ye). For the chair's question on the citation, I would rest it on both the concept and the demonstrated performance, because the concept alone is a proposal and the performance alone would read as engineering, and I would word it so that it credits only the lattice clock and does not reach into Ye's comb, laser-stabilisation or nuclear-clock work.
statement.case_against: The attribution at the edges is still the main weakness. Takamoto and Ido made the first strontium lattice-clock demonstration, Lemonde's group made comparable contributions, and none of them can be named under a two-person credit; a citation worded around the invention and development of the lattice clock leaves them outside, and I have to accept that cost openly. Pearce's remark that the prize should favour a new observational window is a fair challenge, and I cannot prove that a measurement tool carries the same weight as the opening of neutrino astronomy or the completion of the Standard Model. The three-person limit does not force a choice here, since two names are enough, but it does force a decision on who is omitted from B026, and I do not think that decision can be made well. The risk I take seriously is that agreement among members with an atomic-physics vantage, which Lindroth warned about, is a weak guide. Four of us prefer B042 but four do not, and the others see it only as a fallback.

responses.point: Danielsson keeps the Higgs discovery with Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee first because nature answered a half-century question, and he concedes the trio is a leadership proxy for thousands of people.
responses.response: I agree that the scientific weight of the Higgs discovery is not in question and that the 2013 prize left the experiment unrecognised. Where I still part from him is the attribution step, which he acknowledges himself. In round 1 I asked what each of the three actually did in 2012, and I think the committee still has no concrete answer: conception and leadership of two collaborations is not an identifiable original act in the way a magic-wavelength proposal is. His own text says that a prize on a weak attribution is weaker than the physics deserves. I take that sentence as the deciding point. I do not set B026 aside as unworthy, but I will not choose a configuration I cannot defend name by name, and I would need to hear a principle for the three names that survives the objection about spokespersons and analysis leaders before I changed.

responses.point: Pearce prefers IceCube with Halzen and Spiering because it is a discovery of nature with a clean two-name credit, and he accepts that source identification is partial and that Baikal, DUMAND, AMANDA and ANTARES credit is open.
responses.response: His answer clarifies that the issue is not whether I value discoveries of nature, and I do. My concern remains maturity and the credit boundary. The diffuse flux is secure, but the population origin and the single blazar association are still developing, and a citation that names two people for a detector with Baikal and DUMAND lineage will be contested. I also thank him for placing B042 as his first alternative, which suggests our difference is about emphasis, not about a scientific defect in the lattice clock. His disclosed link to Fermi-LAT, which was part of the TXS 0506+056 follow-up, is a collaboration-level link, and I would leave the question of recusal to the committee, but it is a further reason why a configuration without that issue is easier to defend.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B042 but warns that agreement among atomic-physics members is not evidence of merit, and says B026 could outrank it on consequence if a defensible attribution principle appeared.
responses.response: I agree with her warning and have tried to answer it by giving the physical argument and not counting support: the magic-wavelength condition is a distinct principle, and the evidence for it is replication across species and laboratories. On her condition for B026, I would reconsider only if someone states the principle for three names and what each did. Until then I regard the scientific consequence as equal on both sides and the attribution as the deciding difference. I disagree with her that Lemonde and early Sr-clock contributors are an edge case that can be ignored; I would put the Takamoto and Ido priority in the committee's record as an explicit decision.

responses.point: Kroll supports B042, with a citation that includes frequency comparison, and would keep Ye's credit confined to the lattice clock, away from comb and ultrastable-laser work.
responses.response: I agree that Ye's credit must be confined to the lattice clock, and I have kept that boundary in my citation. I would not include frequency comparison in the wording of the citation, since that begins to credit the metrology network and comb links built by many groups, and the 1e-18 performance is already demonstrated within the lattice clock itself. On his remark that the consensus is only moderate in depth, I accept the point: four members prefer B042 and I do not treat that count as a substitute for scientific judgment.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance with Miyazaki, Moodera and Parkin, as a closed physics case with decades of replication, but says Yuasa and Djayaprawira are outside the trio.
responses.response: I accept his argument that tunnel magnetoresistance is distinct from giant magnetoresistance, and I accept the maturity. My view of the credit has not changed: the missing names bear on the coherent MgO step, the main driver of industrial use, and not on the edges. I would also like to know from him whether he would replace Parkin or Miyazaki with Yuasa, because the answer would show whether the trio is a defensible representation. He has said B042 is his first alternative and I appreciate that; if he cannot settle the credit question, I think the committee can reach agreement on the lattice clock without any loss of scientific standard.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that Takamoto, Ido and Lemonde are outside a two-name credit and decide that explicitly.
Whether members outside atomic physics see the magic-wavelength lattice as a new principle, as I do, rather than an incremental step after 2005 and 2012.
Whether a pending redefinition of the second should affect timing; my view is that it should not, but I cannot rule out that others will see it differently.
Whether a defensible three-name principle for B026 can be stated; I have not heard one, and I cannot verify individual roles in ATLAS and CMS.
My own assessment of maturity relies on the supplied record and my reading, not on a detailed check of every clock comparison.
statement.conflict_note: My disclosure is unchanged. I have long-running academic exchanges with Japanese universities, including a University of Tokyo fellowship, and Katori is a Tokyo-based physicist, but no personal or institutional tie to him or to Ye is documented. I have no known connection to Takamoto, Ido or Lemonde. Göran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague, but circuit QED (B033) is not part of my configuration, so I see no recusal issue for myself. I note Johansson's and Kroll's disclosures, and I see no reason for the committee to treat Kroll's stay in Boulder as disqualifying. I also have no tie to the IceCube or Fermi-LAT groups, and I leave the question of Pearce's recusal on B029 to the committee.
